core: Working definition of disease surveillance (CDC): ongoing, systematic collection and analysis of health data to detect and track problems
Data sources: reported cases, laboratory results, emergency department visits, death records
What surveillance watches for: new outbreaks, trends, unusual patterns
Reporting chain: clinics and laboratories report to local/state health agencies, states report to CDC (notifiable diseases, MMWR)
What surveillance enables: early response, planning, evaluation
Limits: depends on reporting; underreporting means not all cases are counted
supporting: Etymology of surveillance (French sur/veiller) and the history of the concept (Langmuir 1963; 1968 World Health Assembly definition)
Surveillance as the first of CDC's 10 Essential Public Health Services (assess and monitor population health)
outOfScope: Epidemiology as a discipline and its methods (sibling topic: epidemiology)
How to appraise the quality of evidence (sibling topic: evidence-in-public-health)
Specific disease-by-disease surveillance details or case studies

claims.claim: Public health surveillance is the ongoing, systematic collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of data regarding a health-related event for use in public health action to reduce morbidity and mortality and to improve health (CDC's working definition).

The essence of public health surveillance is the use of data to monitor health problems to facilitate their prevention or control; surveillance provides and interprets data to facilitate the prevention and control of disease.

Surveillance data come from multiple sources, including notifications of cases from health-care providers, health-care facilities and records (physician offices, hospitals, outpatient departments, emergency departments, laboratories), and death certificates; a disease must be diagnosed and recorded before it can be counted.

Surveillance data are used for immediate public health action, program planning and evaluation, and research hypotheses; they measure the burden of disease, identify populations at high risk, identify new or emerging health concerns, and monitor trends including the detection of epidemics (outbreaks).

In the United States, states maintain lists of notifiable diseases that health-care providers and laboratories must report; reports flow to local and state health agencies, and states report notifiable disease data to CDC, which publishes weekly and annual summaries in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR).

Surveillance has real limitations: for the majority of notifiable diseases, data depend on passive reporting by physicians and other health-care providers, and only a fraction of cases are ever reported (underreporting); surveillance 'need not be perfect to be useful,' and even underreported data can still show trends.

Assessing and monitoring population health status, factors that influence health, and community needs and assets is the first of CDC's 10 Essential Public Health Services — surveillance is public health's core monitoring function.

The term surveillance comes from the French sur (over) and veiller (to watch); Alexander Langmuir's 1963 paper described disease surveillance as continued watchfulness over the distribution and trends of incidence through the systematic collection, consolidation, and evaluation of morbidity and mortality reports and other relevant data.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How complete are surveillance counts? Passive reporting undercounts: for many notifiable diseases only a fraction of cases are ever reported (reporting as low as 9% for some conditions in one cited study), while for rare, serious diseases such as rabies or botulism, reporting may approach 100% of diagnosed cases.
positions: Surveillance numbers understate the true number of cases for most diseases.
For severe, distinctive diseases, counts can be nearly complete.
CDC's position: surveillance need not be perfect to be useful; underreported data can still reveal trends.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the honest middle ground: surveillance is a reliable indicator of trends and changes, not a perfect census; its completeness varies by disease and by reporting behavior, which is why agencies treat quiet data with caution.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft called disease surveillance 'a foundational concept' and framed it as 'a label on a toolbox drawer' — generic boilerplate with no factual surveillance content; discarded entirely.
The draft's vocabulary defined 'disease surveillance' circularly as 'A foundational Public Health concept covered in this lesson' — replaced with a verified, non-circular definition.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition — Lesson 5, Appendix E: Limitations of Notifiable Disease Surveillance and Recommendations for Improvement
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly from archive.cdc.gov 2026-08-22. Supports the lesson's honest-limits section: surveillance 'need not be perfect to be useful'; limitations arise from underreporting, lack of representativeness, and lack of timeliness; although state laws intend every case of a notifiable disease to be reported, 'the reality is otherwise,' and only a fraction of cases of notifiable diseases overall are ever reported (with reporting for some conditions as low as 9% in one cited study, and near-complete reporting for rare, serious diseases like rabies or botulism); underreported data may still be useful for assessing trends. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
